Where it began

Martin James Guptill was born in Auckland on 30 September 1986. After four years at Kelston Boys High School he finished his schooling at Avondale College, playing in the cricket side and serving as a prefect. Cricket ran a little in the family: his cousin, Michael Guptill-Bunce, also played for Auckland.

He represented New Zealand at the Under-19 World Cup in Sri Lanka in 2006, and his first-class debut that March was a lesson in the game's moods. He lasted four balls for nought in the first innings and made 99 in the second.

The player

He opened the batting for New Zealand in Tests, one-day internationals and T20 internationals. His Test debut came against India at Hamilton in March 2009, and he played 47 Tests up to 2016, scoring 2,586 runs at 29.39 with three hundreds, 17 fifties and a best of 189. He also held 50 catches and picked up eight wickets with his part-time bowling.

The white-ball game was where he became famous. On his one-day debut in 2009 he carried his bat for 122 not out against the West Indies, the first New Zealander to make a hundred in his first one-day international. In 2013 he hit back-to-back unbeaten hundreds in England. Then came the 2015 World Cup quarter-final in Wellington, where he made 237 not out from 163 balls against the West Indies, at the time the highest score ever made at a World Cup. He finished that tournament as its top run-scorer, with 547.

What made him special

When he got going he was very hard to stop, and he liked a big stage. He was also durable: he played more than a hundred T20 internationals and was the second batsman to reach 3,000 runs in that format. In Tests the runs came less freely than in the shorter game, but 17 fifties tell you how often he got the side off to a solid start.

Away from the middle

His travels took him to Derbyshire, where he made a double hundred at Bristol in 2015, and to leagues in India, Pakistan, the Caribbean, Sri Lanka and Nepal. In December 2024 he made the first fifty ever scored in the Nepal Premier League. He won the Sir Richard Hadlee Medal for 2011–12, retired from international cricket in January 2025 and in the 2026 New Year Honours was appointed MNZM, the New Zealand Order of Merit, for his services to the game.

And finally

At the 2015 World Cup he made three ducks in the group stage and yet ended up as the leading run-scorer. Cricket rarely forgives a slow start so generously, but it did for him.
